# Nālaka Sutta (Snp 3.11 (PTS Snp 131))

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Nālaka Sutta* (Snp 3.11) is the eleventh discourse of the Mahāvagga in the *Suttanipāta* [Norman 1997-2001; Norman 1983]. It is composed of two distinct sections [Norman 1983; Hazra 1994]. The opening prologue, consisting of twenty introductory stanzas (*vatthugāthā*), recounts the visit of the sage (*isi*) Asita, who descends from the Tusita heaven after witnessing celestial rejoicings at the birth of the Bodhisatta in Kapilavatthu [Norman 1983; Hazra 1994; Guang Xing 2002]. Asita takes the child, foretells (*vyākaraṇa*) his destiny to achieve supreme enlightenment for the liberation of beings, weeps because his own life span will expire before then, and instructs his nephew Nālaka to go forth as an ascetic and await the Buddha's awakening [Norman 1983; Gaffney 2003; Guang Xing 2002]. The second section records Nālaka approaching the newly enlightened Buddha to ask about the practice of the recluse, whereupon the Buddha delivers an exposition on the state of a sage and supreme wisdom (*moneyya*, *moneyyam uttamam padam*) [Norman 1983; von Hinüber 1996].

The second portion of the discourse is widely identified with the *Moneyasute* (or *Moneyasūta*) recommended in Emperor Aśoka's Bairāṭ Edict [Hazra 2002; Norman 1997-2001; von Hinüber 1996; Thomas 1933]. Because the introductory *vatthugāthā* are absent in parallel traditions and show linguistic and metrical features resembling later narrative developments, scholars infer that the prologue was prefixed to the earlier *moneyya* discourse after Aśoka's era [Guang Xing 2002; Norman 1983; Hazra 1994]. In traditional Pali classifications, Buddhaghosa and the *Saddhamma-saṅgaha* repeatedly cite the *Nālaka Sutta*, along with the *Maṅgala*, *Ratana*, and *Tuvataka*, as the representative canonical poems defining the *Sutta* genre within the ninefold classification of teachings (*navaṅga*) [Lamotte 1988; Law 1941; Hazra 1994; Norman 1983]. The text is also cited in the *Cūḷaniddesa*, *Kathāvatthu*, and *Milindapañha*.

Curated passage-level parallels exist in Buddhist Sanskrit literature, notably the *Nālakapraśna* of the Lokottaravāda *Mahāvastu* and the Mūlasarvāstivāda *Saṅghabhedavastu* [Norman 1997-2001; Gaffney 2003]. In the *Mahāvastu*, the Asita legend and Nālaka's questioning are preserved as separate episodes, with the *vatthugāthā* absent from the question section [Norman 1983; Hazra 1994]. DharmaNexus confirms substantial cross-tradition overlap, recording 42 matches with the *Mahāvastu-avadāna*, as well as alignments with Tibetan translations of the *Lalitavistara* and *Samādhirāja Sūtra* [DharmaNexus]. Internally, DharmaNexus registers 26 matching segments shared with the commentary (*Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*) [DharmaNexus], while individual verses parallel ethical maxims found in the *Dhammapada* and *Udānavarga*.
